onboarding: Which sites do you get stuck on most? Pick them — I'll be there 🫂

settings.firstRunSummary: Intermission shows a short pause before the sites you choose. Here is exactly what it keeps.
settings.firstRunStorage: Your settings, chosen sites, and small counters stay in Chrome storage. Settings may sync through Chrome if you use Chrome sync.
settings.firstRunBrowsing: It reads a page's address only to check whether it is a site you chose. Page content and anything you type in the vent room are never saved or sent.
settings.firstRunSharing: No accounts, analytics, ads, or developer servers. Nothing is sold or shared.
settings.permissionNeeded: Sites marked “No access” below still need permission. Click “Allow access to selected sites” above to grant it.
settings.siteAccessGranted: {site} is on and access is granted.
settings.siteAccessRemoved: {site} is off and its access has been removed.
settings.siteAccessRemovePartial: {site} is off, but Chrome still shows access granted. Use Remove to retry, or revoke it in Chrome's extension Site access settings.
settings.siteRemoveFailed: {site} could not be removed because Chrome still shows access granted. Try again, or revoke it in Chrome's extension Site access settings.
settings.permissionToggleDenied: Access wasn't granted, so this site stays off.
settings.intro: Choose the places where you'd like a gentle pause.
settings.sitesDescription: You can change these whenever you like.
settings.youtubeWarning: YouTube is also used for studying, so it isn’t included by default. Add it only if it’s one of your personal traps.
settings.permissionGranted: Access granted. Intermission will show a pause the next time you visit a selected site.
settings.permissionAlreadyGranted: All selected sites already have access.
settings.permissionDenied: Without access, Intermission can’t pause on those sites. You can try again later.
settings.permissionRequestError: Chrome couldn't ask for access. Try again; if it keeps failing, reopen this page.
settings.noEnabledSites: Turn on at least one site first.
settings.siteAddedAccessDenied: {site} added, but it stays off because access wasn't granted. Turn it on to try again.
settings.siteAddedAccessError: {site} added, but Chrome couldn't request access. It stays off; turn it on to try again.
settings.invalidDomain: Enter a website address, like reddit.com.
settings.duplicateDomain: That site is already on your list.
settings.cooldownDescription: If you choose 'Not now', I won't show another pause on that site for this long.
settings.checkinLabel: Ask once after repeated “Not now” choices
settings.checkinDescription: After you choose “Not now” more than 5 times for one site in a day, I’ll ask once whether you want to keep its pause.
settings.timeCheckinDescription: After you use a site continuously for a while, I’ll ask once if you’d like a short break.
settings.footerNote: Your choices are saved in Chrome. No account needed.

popup.settingsDesc: Manage your sites, pause frequency, and check-ins.

interception.greeting: Before you go in, want to pause with me for a minute?
interception.notNowResponse: Okay. I'm here if you need me 🌿
interception.continueCheckin: Is this site's pause helping you?
interception.continueCheckinHint: You've chosen 'Not now' several times today. Would you like to keep the pause or turn it off for this site?
interception.timeCheckinTitle: You’ve been here a while. Want a short break, or would you like to keep going?
interception.keepPauseResponse: Got it, keeping the pause active 🌿
interception.disableSitePause: Turn it off for this site
interception.disabledSitePauseResponse: Pause turned off for this site 🌱
interception.breathingPrepTitle: Take a moment to settle in.
interception.breathingPrepHint: Get comfortable. Breathe as long as you want—there’s no rush.
interception.breathingHint: Breathe in gently as the lungs expand; breathe out slowly as they contract. Keep it comfortable.
interception.breathingFiveMinHint: You've been breathing for 5 whole minutes! Want to do it again, or head back to work?
interception.returning: Taking a moment, then heading back...
interception.returnFailed: Chrome couldn't open a new tab. You can try again, or stay on this page.

0.text: Absolute zero (0 K, −273.15°C) is the lowest temperature on the thermodynamic scale; particles still retain quantum zero-point motion.
The mathematical concept of zero (0) was developed in ancient India, revolutionizing mathematics and computing.
O-negative red blood cells are often used for emergency transfusions when a patient’s blood type is not yet known; they are commonly called the universal red-cell donor type.

1.text: The heart works continuously throughout life, alternating between contraction and relaxation with every beat.
A single star—our Sun—holds 99.86% of all the mass in the entire solar system.
An octopus has only 1 central brain, but two-thirds of its neurons reside independently in its arms.

2.text: The left human lung is somewhat smaller than the right lung and has two lobes instead of three, leaving space for the heart.
Coca-Cola is not officially distributed in North Korea or Cuba under the company’s ordinary distribution network; availability through unofficial channels can vary.

Some woodpeckers can peck at very high rates. Their skull and beak form a specialized structure that withstands repeated impacts; the popular claim that spongy skull bones act as shock absorbers is misleading.

3.text: Octopuses and squids have 3 hearts; two pump blood through the gills, while the third circulates oxygenated blood through the body.
Bees have 3 small additional eyes on top of their head called ocelli, helping them detect polarized light and navigate.
Earth is the 3rd planet from the Sun, and currently the only known celestial body in the universe supporting life.

4.text: Cows have 4 distinct digestive compartments in their stomach to ferment and break down tough fibrous grass.
A mammalian heart has 4 chambers; normal anatomy keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood streams separate.
Horses sleep primarily in short intervals totaling a few hours a day, often while standing, though deep REM sleep requires lying down.

5.text: Most sea stars have 5 arms and lack a centralized blood circulatory system, using a hydraulic water-vascular system for movement and feeding.
The five interlocking Olympic rings symbolize the union of the five continents, as described by the Olympic movement.
The little finger contributes to grip strength and hand function, but it does not provide anything close to half of total grip strength.

6.text: Adult insects have six legs — one pair on each of the thorax's three segments. Larvae like caterpillars grow extra fleshy legs, and a few species have fewer.
Bees build honeycombs using hexagonal cells, a naturally efficient geometry that maximizes perimeter shared between neighboring walls.
Carbon has atomic number 6; its ability to form four stable covalent bonds makes it the foundation of all known organic chemistry.

7.text: Both humans and towering giraffes have the exact same number of neck vertebrae: exactly 7 bones.
A prism disperses white light into a continuous spectrum, traditionally described as seven colors.
The number 7 features in widely recognized traditional lists, including common 7-continent models and the classical Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

8.text: An octopus has 8 arms lined with hundreds of sensitive suckers that can touch and chemically sense substances in the water.
Most spiders have 8 eyes arranged in patterns on their head, though visual acuity varies widely among different families.
Sunlight leaving the surface of the Sun takes approximately 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel 93 million miles to Earth.

9.text: Human pregnancy lasts approximately 38 weeks from conception (about 40 weeks from the last menstrual period), roughly spanning 9 calendar months.
Our solar system was officially classified as having 9 planets for over 75 years until Pluto was reclassified in 2006.
A mathematical curiosity of 9: any integer is divisible by 9 if and only if the sum of its digits is divisible by 9.

10.text: The decimal base-10 numbering system used globally today is widely believed to have originated from humans counting on their 10 fingers.
Neon has atomic number 10; when an electric current passes through it, this noble gas glows a brilliant reddish-orange.
Canada, the second-largest country on Earth by land area, is composed of exactly 10 provinces and 3 territories.

11.text: In July 1969, the historic Apollo 11 mission succeeded in landing the very first humans on the surface of the Moon.
The Sun’s activity follows an approximately 11-year cycle from one solar minimum to the next, although the cycle length varies.
Sodium has atomic number 11; it is an essential dietary mineral necessary for transmitting nerve impulses in the body.

12.text: The human rib cage is formed of 12 symmetrical pairs of ribs (24 ribs in total) guarding the heart and lungs.
In human history, exactly 12 astronauts have had the privilege of walking on the lunar surface.
A solar year contains about 12.37 lunar phase cycles (new moon to new moon), which helps explain the historical use of 12-month lunar and lunisolar calendars.

13.text: A 'baker's dozen' equals 13, traditionally explained as bakers adding an extra loaf to avoid historical penalties for selling underweight bread.
Aluminium has atomic number 13; it is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust, making up about 8% of its weight.
The original United States national flag featured 13 stars and 13 alternating stripes honoring the 13 founding colonies.

14.text: There are only 14 mountains on planet Earth that rise above 8,000 meters (26,247 feet) above sea level.
A traditional Shakespearean or Petrarchan sonnet is strictly structured as a poetic form of 14 rhyming lines.
Silicon has atomic number 14; its semiconducting properties serve as the physical heart of all modern computing chips.

15.text: Phosphorus has atomic number 15; it forms the vital structural backbone of human DNA and cellular energy (ATP).
In professional tennis scoring, winning the very first rally awards a score of 15 points.
Light is so fast that in just 15 nanoseconds, it travels a distance of over 4.5 meters (15 feet).

16.text: A standard game of chess starts with 16 pieces per player: 8 pawns, 2 rooks, 2 knights, 2 bishops, 1 queen, and 1 king.
Oxygen, the element that drives cellular respiration across most terrestrial life, has an atomic mass of roughly 16.
Pure elemental sulfur has atomic number 16 and is odorless; the pungent smell often associated with matches or volcanic gases comes from sulfur compounds like sulfur dioxide.

17.text: Some periodical cicada species live underground as nymphs for about 17 years before emerging together as adults for a short time.
Chlorine has atomic number 17; it is universally utilized across the world to purify drinking water supplies from deadly pathogens.
Mathematicians proved that a standard 9x9 Sudoku puzzle requires a minimum of 17 clues to possess a unique solvable answer.

18.text: Argon has atomic number 18; it is an inert noble gas that makes up roughly 0.93% of Earth's atmosphere, more than CO2.
A standard full golf course consists of 18 holes, a convention established at the Old Course at St Andrews in the 19th century.
In many countries, 18 is the minimum voting age, but the legal voting age varies by country and sometimes by type of election.

19.text: Potassium has atomic number 19; this electrolyte is essential for cellular water balance and maintaining regular human heartbeat rhythms.
Halley’s Comet takes about 75–76 years to orbit the Sun and was last seen from Earth in 1986; its next predicted return is in 2061.
19 is a twin prime paired with 17, representing two consecutive odd numbers that are both prime.

20.text: Children develop 20 primary (baby) teeth, which are gradually shed as permanent adult teeth emerge.
Calcium has atomic number 20; it is the most abundant mineral in the human body, vital for bone density and muscle contraction.
An icosahedron is a regular convex polyhedron featuring exactly 20 identical equilateral triangular faces.

21.text: Earth's breathable atmosphere consists of approximately 21% clean elemental oxygen, with the remaining 78% being nitrogen.
The pips (dots) on all six sides of a standard gaming die sum up to exactly 21 (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6).
Scandium has atomic number 21; adding small amounts of it to aluminum creates strong, weldable alloys used in specialized aerospace parts.

22.text: The human skull is constructed of 22 individual bones: 8 cranial bones safeguarding the brain and 14 facial bones.
Titanium has atomic number 22 and is about 45% lighter than steel with a comparable strength-to-weight ratio, resisting corrosion in harsh environments.
The regulation distance between the two wickets on a standard cricket pitch is precisely 22 yards.

23.text: Most human nucleated somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes (23 pairs), with one set inherited from each biological parent; mature red blood cells have no nucleus, and sperm and egg cells normally contain 23.
Earth’s axial tilt (about 23.4°) changes the angle and duration of sunlight through the year, producing the seasons.
Vanadium has atomic number 23; adding a trace amount to steel doubles its tensile strength, widely used in armor plating.

24.text: Earth takes 24 hours to complete one rotation relative to the Sun (a mean solar day), which forms the basis for modern daily timekeeping.
Pure, unalloyed gold is officially rated at 24 karats, containing 99.9% fine elemental gold.
The human spine contains 24 articulating vertebrae that allow us to twist, bend, and stand upright.

25.text: Manganese has atomic number 25; it acts as the essential core catalyst in plants that splits water molecules to generate oxygen.
A 25th anniversary milestone is traditionally and globally celebrated as the 'Silver Jubilee'.
A standard United States quarter coin is valued at exactly 25 cents.

26.text: Iron (atomic number 26) is the central atom in the heme group of hemoglobin, allowing red blood cells to bind and transport oxygen through the body.
The standard modern English alphabet contains exactly 26 distinct phonetic letters.
An official marathon race covers a historic distance of 26 miles and 385 yards (42.195 kilometers).

27.text: The Moon completes one full sidereal orbit around Earth in approximately 27.3 days.
Cobalt has atomic number 27; it yields distinctive deep blue pigments and forms the essential metallic core of Vitamin B12.
Uranus has 29 known moons. Twenty-seven are named after characters from Shakespeare and Alexander Pope; the two newest are still unnamed.

28.text: Nickel (atomic number 28) is a key magnetic transition metal, forming a significant component of Earth’s metallic core alongside iron.
A standard 'double-six' set of classic dominoes comprises precisely 28 distinct gaming tiles.
February is the shortest month of the modern Gregorian calendar, having 28 days during common non-leap years.

29.text: Copper (atomic number 29) is a premier electrical conductor; while pure silver conducts slightly better, copper is the universal standard for electrical wiring.
In the Gregorian calendar, a year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except century years that are not divisible by 400.
The synodic lunar month, measuring the time from one new moon to the next, averages approximately 29.53 days.

30.text: Zinc has atomic number 30; it is an essential trace element necessary for DNA synthesis, immune defense, and rapid wound healing.
A 30-year anniversary is traditionally associated with pearls in many cultural gift conventions.
Four calendar months in the Gregorian year—April, June, September, and November—have exactly 30 days.

31.text: Seven months across the calendar year (January, March, May, July, August, October, December) boast exactly 31 days.
Gallium has atomic number 31; this metal remains solid at room temperature but melts directly into liquid in the palm of your warm hand (29.76°C).
In hot weather, thermal expansion makes the Eiffel Tower a few millimeters taller. Uneven heating by the Sun can also make its top shift along a path about 15 centimeters in diameter.

32.text: A complete set of permanent adult teeth can include up to 32 teeth, including the four wisdom teeth.
On the Fahrenheit temperature scale, pure water freezes into solid ice at precisely 32 degrees under standard atmospheric pressure.
Germanium has atomic number 32; it is a critical semiconductor used in wide-angle camera optics and high-speed fiber communications.

33.text: Human babies are born with 33 individual vertebrae in their spine before several naturally fuse during skeletal maturation.
Arsenic has atomic number 33; historically dubbed the 'King of Poisons', it has also played roles in glassmaking and semiconductors.
Classic full-length 12-inch vinyl LP records spin at a standard rotational speed of 33⅓ revolutions per minute.

34.text: Selenium has atomic number 34; named after Selene, the Greek goddess of the Moon, it acts as a cellular antioxidant.
34 is the ninth Fibonacci number, appearing in the spiral arrangements of sunflower seed heads and pinecones.
Hypothermia begins below 35°C (95°F): 32–35°C is mild, 28–32°C is moderate, and below 28°C is severe.

35.text: Bromine has atomic number 35; it is the only nonmetallic element on the periodic table that is naturally liquid at room temperature.
Under the United States Constitution, a citizen must be at least 35 years of age to be eligible for election as President.
A 35-year anniversary is traditionally associated with coral or jade in common gift lists.

36.text: A standard European roulette wheel features numbers from 1 to 36, plus a single green zero pocket, totaling 37 pockets.
Krypton is a noble gas used in some specialized lighting applications, including certain high-intensity lamps.
36 is mathematically rare: it is simultaneously both a square number (6 x 6) and a triangular number (the sum of 1 through 8).

37.text: 37°C (98.6°F) is a traditional reference value for average human body temperature, but normal temperature varies among people and with measurement method and time of day.
Rubidium has atomic number 37; it is a soft alkali metal so reactive that it spontaneously ignites when exposed to atmospheric air.
Every three-digit repdigit (111, 222, …, 999) is divisible by 37.

38.text: Strontium has atomic number 38; its energetic electron transitions produce the vibrant, deep crimson red colors seen in fireworks.
The Korean Demilitarized Zone lies near the 38th parallel, but its boundary does not follow the parallel exactly.
Pregnancy lasts about 38 weeks from fertilization, or about 40 weeks when dated from the first day of the last menstrual period.

39.text: Yttrium has atomic number 39; this rare earth metal is essential in manufacturing spark plugs, camera lenses, and superconductors.
The Protestant Old Testament canon contains 39 books; Catholic and Orthodox canons contain additional books.
At an average rate of about 75 beats per minute, a resting adult heart would beat roughly 39 million times in a year; the actual number varies.

40.text: -40 degrees is the singular temperature point where both the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales read the exact same number (-40°C = -40°F).
Zirconium has atomic number 40; its exceptional corrosion resistance and low neutron absorption make it the premier coating for nuclear fuel rods.
A 40th anniversary is widely celebrated as a Ruby Jubilee in traditional anniversary lists.

41.text: Niobium has atomic number 41; it is an extraordinary superconducting metal that powers high-field magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanners.
41 is a celebrated prime number: Euler's famous polynomial (n² + n + 41) yields consecutive primes for every integer from 0 to 39.
41 is the starting constant in Euler's famous prime-generating polynomial (x² + x + 41), which produces prime numbers for all integers from 0 to 39.

42.text: In Douglas Adams' iconic sci-fi classic 'The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy', 42 is the ultimate answer to life, the universe, and everything.
A primary rainbow appears when sunlight is refracted, internally reflected, and refracted again in raindrops; its red edge is seen about 42° from the antisolar point.
Molybdenum is a trace element required by enzymes involved in nitrogen metabolism; nitrogen fixation is carried out by certain microorganisms, often in association with plants.

43.text: Technetium was the first chemical element to be artificially produced; tiny amounts also occur naturally in some uranium ores.
The human face has dozens of muscles that work together to produce a wide range of facial expressions.
43 is a prime number: its only positive divisors are 1 and 43.

44.text: The international direct-dial telephone calling country code for the United Kingdom is +44.
Ruthenium has atomic number 44; this rare platinum-group metal is used to harden platinum and palladium for wear-resistant electrical contacts.
In 44 BC, Roman dictator Julius Caesar was assassinated on the historic Ides of March.

45.text: Rhodium has atomic number 45; it is one of the rarest, most corrosion-resistant, and expensive precious metals on Earth.
A 45th anniversary is traditionally honored as a Sapphire Jubilee in recognized gift lists.
Classic 7-inch vinyl record singles were engineered to rotate on turntables at exactly 45 revolutions per minute.

46.text: Most human nucleated somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes (23 pairs), with one set inherited from each biological parent; mature red blood cells have no nucleus, and sperm and egg cells normally contain 23.
Palladium (atomic number 46) can absorb vast quantities of hydrogen gas at room temperature, acting like a chemical sponge.
Human chromosome 1 is the largest, spanning roughly 249 million DNA base pairs and representing 8% of total cellular DNA.

47.text: Silver has atomic number 47; of all elements on Earth, pure silver exhibits the highest electrical and thermal conductivity.
The Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn are currently about 23.4° north and south of the equator, roughly 46.8° of latitude apart.
Silver has atomic number 47; its chemical symbol 'Ag' comes from 'argentum', the Latin word for silver.

48.text: Cadmium has atomic number 48; its neutron-absorbing qualities make it ideal for nuclear reactor safety control rods.
The contiguous continental United States consists of 48 adjoining states, excluding only Alaska and Hawaii.
In the 2nd century CE, Ptolemy’s Almagest described 48 constellations known to Greco-Roman astronomy; many of these remain in use today.

49.text: 49 is a clean perfect square: 7 multiplied by itself equals 49.
The 49th parallel forms a long section of the land boundary between Canada and the United States, but not the entire border.
In Tibetan Buddhist tradition, the intermediate 'Bardo' transition state between physical death and rebirth lasts 49 days.

50.text: A 50-year celebration is historically and globally heralded as the magnificent 'Golden Jubilee'.
Bronze (an alloy usually made from copper and tin) became important in different regions at different times; the Bronze Age began more than 5,000 years ago in some parts of the world.
The United States is made up of exactly 50 states, permanently honored by the 50 white stars emblazoned upon the national flag.

general_facts.text: In English traditional lore, a group of crows is sometimes called a murder, and a group of owls is called a parliament.
There's a species of frog that can freeze solid in winter and thaw back to life in spring.
Scotland's national animal is the unicorn.
A typical cumulus cloud can contain around a million pounds of water droplets and still float suspended in the atmosphere.
Polar bears have black skin under their white fur.
Some turtles can breathe through their cloaca.
Under certain conditions, warm water has been observed to freeze faster than cold water; this is known as the Mpemba effect, and scientists continue to study its exact causes.
Humans and bananas share many basic cellular genes because all life shares ancient biological ancestry, though popular claims of a simple '60% identical DNA' oversimplify genetic comparisons.
The estimated number of possible unique chess games (the Shannon number, roughly 10¹²⁰) is vastly greater than the estimated number of atoms in the observable universe (about 10⁸⁰).
Crows can recognize individual human faces and can communicate perceived threats to other crows in their group through social learning.
Bananas are naturally slightly radioactive because of their potassium.
Sea otters are sometimes observed holding paws or wrapping themselves in kelp while sleeping to avoid drifting apart in ocean currents.
A group of flamingos is sometimes playfully called a flamboyance.
Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings, a unique result of intestinal elasticity that may help prevent them from rolling off rocks when marking territory.
Cats usually have fewer toes on their back paws than their front paws—four in back, five in front.
A lightning channel can be much hotter than the surface of the sun, but only for a very brief moment.
A day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus.
Three-toed sloths can slow their heart rate to hold their breath underwater for up to 40 minutes, easily outlasting many marine animals.
Butterflies can taste with their feet.
The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 lasted less than an hour.
A shrimp's heart is located in its cephalothorax, the fused head and thorax region of its body.
Thorough hand-washing with soap should take at least 20 seconds to effectively remove pathogens—about the time it takes to hum 'Happy Birthday' twice.
